value: 1.9 ± 0.3 (mean ± s.d.) times more Calanus spp. were attracted to the unpolarized-light trap than to the polarized-light trap; trap intensities were not equal (see conditions)
method: behavioural: paired plankton light traps, each lit by an LED flashlight showing polarized or unpolarized light, counts of Calanus caught
conditions: Field experiment 4 to 13 April 2013 at the end of a dock, Austevoll Research Station, Norway; paired traps 2 m apart at 30 m depth, 23:00 to 04:00, 90 min each, 15 paired sets (one replicate each); light spectra measured 400 to 700 nm; intensity (420 to 700 nm) 0.7 ± 0.4 in the unpolarized trap and 1.2 ± 0.5 × 10^-11 µE cm^-2 nm^-1 s^-1 in the polarized trap, although the authors write that the design ensured equal intensity, and they do not discuss the difference; partial polarization 68.1 ± 11.4% (polarized trap) and 15.4 ± 7.9% (unpolarized trap); one-sample t-test on arcsine-transformed ratios, p = 0.010; the authors limit the conclusion to these low intensities; animals not identified to species (the authors say C. finmarchicus and C. helgolandicus typically occur in the area at about 9:1)

source.title: The copepod Calanus spp. (Calanidae) is repelled by polarized light

where: Results, first paragraph (ratio sentence); the authors' reading 'Calanus spp. displayed negative polarotaxis.' is the first sentence of the Discussion; intensity and polarization from Methods
quote: More Calanus spp. were attracted to the unpolarized traps than to the polarized traps by a ratio of 1.9 ± 0.3 (mean ± s.d.).
note: Genus-level group record (two species mixed, not separable), so grade g. Free-living wild animals at depth, not a restrained preparation. The authors read the result as negative polarotaxis at low intensity; because the polarized trap was also the brighter one on average, the trap test does not separate polarization from intensity; it does not show which photoreceptors drive it, nor that Calanus resolves the polarization pattern. Crossref licence CC BY 4.0 (vor).

value: 530 nm (green) was the most attractive narrowband light by point estimate and broadband white (425 to 750 nm) was equally attractive; 505 nm and 560 nm were also significantly more attractive than the 410 nm baseline, and 530 nm was not tested against them
method: behavioural: groups of three krill in an 80 L tank, number in the illuminated section nearest an LED lamp counted every 30 s over 5-min trials
conditions: Laboratory at 8 °C; krill wild-caught weekly in January to February 2016 (150 to 180 m, Langenuen, western Norway); eight replicate groups of three krill (unbalanced design); nine narrowband LEDs 410, 425, 448, 470, 505, 530, 560, 590, 625 nm plus broadband white, so peak position is bounded by that stimulus set; light intensity had no direct effect on attraction but raised swimming activity; attraction to 505 (printed 503) nm, 530 nm and white light each differed from the 410 nm baseline (odds ratios 2.94 to 3.65, p < 0.005) and 560 nm also differed (range 2.09 to 3.65); no pairwise test between attractive wavelengths; intensities 0.25, 0.5 and 1.0 µE m-2 s-1, with no matching procedure across wavelengths described; 8 replicate groups planned, data set unbalanced (S1 Table)

quote: The most attractive individual wavelength was 530 nm (green light), while broadband (425–750 nm) white light was an equally attractive light source.
note: Behavioural preference, not a photoreceptor peak: attraction depends on intensity and spectral scoring in the arena and cannot be read as lambda max. Krill gathered near the lamp section may also reflect general activity. Crossref licence CC BY 4.0 (vor).

value: perceives polarized light; the authors conclude this capability contributes to perceiving the radiance and/or spectral gradient that sandhoppers use as a compass cue for zonal orientation
method: behavioural: directional choices of single sandhoppers released in a transparent bowl under an artificial sky (opaline Plexiglas dome) with a blue gelatin filter and a grey control or linear polarizing filter over half the surface
conditions: Adults collected on a sandy beach in the Regional Natural Park of Migliarino near Pisa, Italy, May 2020, tested within 5 days; groups of 8 to 10 released, each animal released once and its heading taken 2 min later; radially oriented animals 112 of 180 (62%) under the grey control and 155 of 239 (65%) under the polarizing filter, a difference that was not significant (G = 0.306, df = 1); mean directions and vector lengths are given in figures only

source.authors: Ugolini A, Hariyama T, Wilcockson DC, Mercatelli L
source.title: The use of polarized light in the zonal orientation of the sandhopper Talitrus saltator (Montagu)

where: Abstract (read on two fetches of the Zoological Letters article page); animal counts from Results
quote: Our experiments confirm that T. saltator perceives polarized light and highlight that this visual capability determines the perception, or perhaps the increase, of the radiance and/or spectral gradient and their use as compass cues in the zonal orientation.
note: The abstract's 'perceives polarized light' rests on orientation in a confined artificial-sky bowl, where the polarization gradient and a radiance gradient are not fully separable (the authors write 'or perhaps the increase'). Not a field test and not an e-vector compass result: the abstract states the species does not use the e-vector as a compass cue on the sea-land axis. Crossref licence CC BY 4.0.

value: negative phototaxis under blue (450 nm) LED light and under full-spectrum (400 to 750 nm) light; no noticeable movement under red (630 nm) LED light
method: behavioural: movement of adult urchins away from or toward LED sources of different colour placed at one or both sides of a tank
conditions: Adults about 12 months old, test size 6 to 8 cm; phototaxis groups of three black and three white urchins in four biological replicates; LED illuminance at 30 cm was not matched (full-spectrum 940 lux, red 360 lux, blue 30 lux), so colour and brightness are not separated; single-source and paired-source trials; blue also gave the strongest covering response and slowest righting

note: Urchins have no eyes; light is sensed by photoreceptors elsewhere on the body, so this is a whole-animal light-avoidance result and not evidence of image-forming vision. The red null is for one LED colour at lower, unmatched illuminance. Crossref licence CC BY 4.0 (vor).

conditions: Laboratory; small urchins 1 to 2 cm test diameter (10.3 ± 1.3 mm), body weight 0.6 ± 0.2 g; N = 5 per treatment; three light environments, none (0 lx), low (24 to 209 lx) and high (252 to 2,280 lx); average velocity and distance covered did not differ among the three intensities (P > 0.05)
